prize_parts.citation: for empirical analysis of how technology and trade exposure reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality

statement.case_for: B038 combines new measurement, credible causal design and a conceptual framework, and it has more than a decade of replication behind it. The China-shock papers showed that trade exposure produces persistent local adjustment costs. The task-based account of technology explained job polarisation and wage inequality. Together they changed research and policy on technological change and globalisation, which are central distributional questions. Both strands rest on new and carefully assembled data and on designs the field has adopted as standard. This resembles the historical work I value, where archival or administrative evidence is combined with modern causal econometrics. I keep it first after reading the openings. It is the only candidate that a majority of colleagues placed in their top five or higher, although I do not treat support counts as scientific merit. The substantive arguments from colleagues have not shown that the core attribution is wrong. They have shown where the prize rationale needs care.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the entry bundles two programmes, the task framework and the trade-shock evidence, with partly different lineages. The task framework draws on contributors outside the credited names, such as Levy and Murnane. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects, and the shift-share identification strategy, are still debated. There is also thematic proximity to the 2023, 2024 and 2025 prizes on labour-market history, institutions and technological change. A citation that claims too much of the task literature would be vulnerable. A citation limited to what Autor, Dorn and Hanson established is defensible.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B038 second but proposes Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that Katz's long-running work on skill demand and wage structure belongs in the credited set, while Dorn is a real co-author whom the three-name cap leaves out.
responses.response: I take Katz's contribution to wage structure and the education-technology race seriously, and I agree the task framework has wider ancestry than this entry captures. But the prize rationale I propose is about local labour-market adjustment to trade and technology exposure. The empirical core of that rationale is the Autor-Dorn-Hanson body of work, and a citation without Dorn would misdescribe who produced the evidence. Katz also appears on B002, so putting him here would blur two separate cases. I would revisit this if the committee wanted a citation centred on skill-biased change and wage structure. In that case Katz would be central and Dorn's place would be the contested one.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B038 fifth. He notes the overlap with Acemoglu's recognised work on tasks and technology, the remaining questions about the China-shock estimates, and the subtle credit boundary around Katz.
responses.response: The overlap is a fair concern and it argues for a narrow citation. The recognised institutions-and-prosperity work is about long-run institutional determinants of prosperity. The B038 contribution is about measured labour-market adjustment to specific trade and technology shocks, which is a different object and a different identification strategy. On magnitudes, I agree they are contested. But the debate concerns the size and persistence of effects, and the research design and the basic finding of concentrated, lasting local adjustment costs have been absorbed by the field. I do not think uncertainty about magnitudes should count against a discovery of this kind.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B038 seventh. He asks whether shift-share instruments withstand current scrutiny, notes that the task framework owes much to scholars not listed, and points to overlap with the 2024 and 2025 prizes.
responses.response: I accept that the shift-share critique is real and that it should shape the citation. My view is that the econometric literature has refined the conditions for valid identification without overturning the main findings. The evidence rests on several outcomes, on pre-trends and on follow-up studies that use different designs. That is stronger than the reliance on one instrument that the critique implies. I agree the task framework should not be credited wholesale to the named laureates, so my citation focuses on the empirical analysis of exposure and adjustment. I would be uncomfortable giving more weight to the 2024 and 2025 overlap than to the substance, since those prizes addressed different questions.

responses.point: Teorell places B002 first and B038 fifth. He values work that combines measurement with credible causal design, and he is cautious about the young B002 agenda and about the attribution of the task-based line to Autor alone.
responses.response: We agree on the criterion of measurement and causal design together, and B002 meets it well. My difference is about maturity. B038 has more than a decade of replication, critique and extension, while the neighbourhood-effects findings in B002 are still being tested for long-run robustness and for dependence on restricted data. On the task line, I agree it is closely tied to Autor and has a wider lineage, which is why I do not want the citation to rest on it. If the committee judged B002 mature enough, I would regard it as the natural alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would treat the trade-shock and task strands as one coherent contribution or as two, which affects both the citation wording and the choice of Dorn versus Katz.
How far long-run persistence and the shift-share identification debate should lower confidence in the magnitude of the China-shock effects.
Whether proximity to the recent prizes on labour-market history, institutions and technological change should reduce appetite for B038 relative to B002 or B027.
Whether B027 should be preferred on maturity grounds, and whether Besley belongs in that grouping. I ranked it second in my opening but it has little support among colleagues.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. None of the B038 candidates are among my listed co-authors or institutional connections. I work on electrification, railroads and labour outcomes, so there is thematic proximity to technology and labour-market change, but that is not a personal connection. I share Lund affiliation with committee colleagues, which does not relate to any candidate.
